:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^3 - x^2$ at the point $(1,0)$ is given by $y=px+q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the values of $p$ and $q.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=x^3 - x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-{x}^{2})=3{x}^{2}-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1, 0){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=3-2=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =-(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-1$ and $q=1.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=2{x}^{2}$ at the point $(2,8)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $p+q.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{2}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2})=4x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,8):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(2)=4(2)=8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{8}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-8 & =-\frac{1}{8}(x-2) \\ 8y-64 & =-x+2 \\ x+8y & =66.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p+q=8+66=74.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=2{x}^{5}-2x$ at the point $(1,0)$ is given by $y=ax+b$ where $a$ and $b$ are constants. Find the value of $a+b.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{5}-2x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{5}-2x)=10{x}^{4}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=10(1)^{4}-2=8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{8}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =-\frac{1}{8}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{8}+\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a+b=-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{8}=0.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}$ at the point $(1,4)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $q-p.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{-1/2}) \\  & =-2{x}^{-3/2} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{{1}^{3}}}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ 2y-8 & =x-1 \\ x-2y & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q-p=-7-(-2)=-5.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}-x$ at the point $(1,3)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $p-q.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}-x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}-x\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{-2}-x) \\  & =-8{x}^{-3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=-8(1)^{-3}-1=-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(3) & =\frac{1}{9}(x-1) \\ 9y-27 & =x-1 \\ x-9y & =-26.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p-q=-9-(-26)=17.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{4}{x}$ at the point $(1,4)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $p+q.$

Let $f(x)=\frac{4}{x}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{4}{x}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{-1}) \\  & =-4{x}^{-2} \\  & =-\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m &={f}^{′}(1)=-\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(4) & =\frac{1}{4}(x-(1)) \\ 4y-16 & =x-1 \\ x-4y & =-15.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p+q=-4+(-15)=-19.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y = 2x^3 -x^2$ at the point $(1,1).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3-x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
f'(x)  =6x^2 -2x
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
m=f'(1) = 6(1)^2 - 2(1) = 4
$$

$$

$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x) = 2\sqrt{x} -4x$ at the point $(1,-2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}-4x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}-4x) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

     

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1) = (1)^{-1/2} - 4 = -3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = \dfrac 1 3.
$$

The equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y+2 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{1}{3}-2 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{7}{3} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(7,0).$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The equation of the normal line to the curve $y = f(x)$ at the point $P(x_1,y_1),$ in point-slope form, is given by

$$
y - y_1 = m (x - x_1), \hspace{1cm} m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}.
$$

Here, $m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}$ because the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line, and $f'(x_1)$ represents the slope of the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at the point $(x_1,y_1).$

For example, suppose we want to compute the equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^2$ at the point $A(1,1).$ This normal line is the dashed line shown below, which is perpendicular to the solid tangent line. 

![](images/31/31ba09ff14e5bd485794f283c5d6a5b087b6c21fdb9242af01b75ec8e8744e0d.png)

Since $y=x^2,$ we have $f(x)=x^2.$ We begin by calculating the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) 		 = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(x^2)= 2x
$$

At $A(1,1),$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
f'(1) 	= 2(1) = 2.
$$

However, we want the normal line, and the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
m = -\dfrac{1}{f'(1)} = -\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

 

Finally, we work out the equation of the normal line using the point-slope form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+1 \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the normal line is $y=-\dfrac x 2 + \dfrac 3 2.$ We could also write this in standard form as $x+2y=3.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x) = 2\sqrt{x} -4x$ at the point $(1,-2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}-4x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}-4x) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

     

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1) = (1)^{-1/2} - 4 = -3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = \dfrac 1 3.
$$

The equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y+2 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{1}{3}-2 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{7}{3} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(7,0).$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find, in point-slope form, the equation of the line that passes through the point $(6,2)$ and has a slope of $4.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Using $m=4$ and $(x_1,y_1) = (6,2)$, we substitute into the point-slope formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-2 & =4(x-6)\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding a Point-Slope Equation Given a Slope and a Point

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find, in point-slope form, the equation of the straight line that passes through the points $(5,7)$ and $(1,-1).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We know that the line passes through the point $(5,7),$ so we can use $(x_1,y_1) = (5,7)$ in our point-slope formula. All that remains is to compute $m,$ and we can do this using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}=\frac{-1-7}{1-5}=\frac{-8}{-4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $m=2$ and the point $(x_1,y_1) = (5,7)$ into the point-slope formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-7 & =2(x-5)\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding a Point-Slope Equation Given Two Points

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Calculate the equation of the straight line that passes through the points $(1,10)$ and $(3,-2),$ giving your final answer in slope-intercept form.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we will construct the point-slope formula for the line. Then, we will simplify the point-slope formula into slope-intercept form.

We start by computing the slope $m$ using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}=\frac{-2-10}{3-1}=\frac{-12}{2}=-6\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $m=-6$ and the point $(x_1,y_1) = (1,10)$ into the point-slope formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-10 & =-6(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the equation into slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-10 & =-6(x-1) \\ y-10 & =-6x+6 \\ y & =-6x+16\end{aligned}
$$
